item.title: Security Signal Weekly: June 20-26, 2026

xhtml:img.alt: Security Signal Weekly editorial graphic with the series title, signal bars, and cybersecurity alert panels in the CybersecKyle site colors.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: The week's biggest cybersecurity stories, filtered for defender impact, patch urgency, active exploitation, and what IT teams should actually do next.
item.content:encoded:
Overview

This week was less about one headline vulnerability and more about the systems we quietly trust: network controllers, voice platforms, PLM tools, firewalls, browser extensions, AI agent skills, proxy infrastructure, remote management tools, and malware triage pipelines. The through line is simple enough: attackers keep looking for places where operational trust is high and day-to-day scrutiny is low.

Reality check: The practical work this week is not just patching. It is proving exposure, rotating access, checking for persistence, and deciding which trusted integrations deserve to stay trusted.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. Ubiquiti UniFi OS flaws move from patch queue to active-exploitation queue

What happened: CISA added three Ubiquiti UniFi OS vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after evidence of active exploitation. Bishop Fox’s technical writeup explains how CVE-2026-34908, CVE-2026-34909, and CVE-2026-34910 can be chained into unauthenticated command execution, with UniFi OS Server fixed in version 5.0.8 or later.

Why it matters: UniFi gear often lives in small business, MSP, branch office, and prosumer environments where it is treated as infrastructure plumbing. A management-plane RCE chain is not just a device bug; it can become control over network visibility, routing, and the systems that define trust for the rest of the environment.

Action:

  • Inventory UniFi OS Server, Cloud Gateway, Dream Machine, NVR, and related UniFi appliances, then confirm they are on the vendor-fixed releases.
  • Remove UniFi management from direct internet exposure and restrict administration to trusted networks or VPN paths.
  • Use the Bishop Fox guidance or other safe detection logic to identify vulnerable instances, then review device logs and accounts for unusual access.

2. Lantronix EDS5000 exploitation shows how fast patch reverse-engineering can move

What happened: CISA’s June 23 KEV update also covered CVE-2025-67038 in Lantronix EDS5000 devices. Forescout Vedere Labs later described Chaya_006 activity exploiting the Lantronix command-injection flaw after the vendor patch existed but before public technical details were released.

Why it matters: Serial-to-IP converters and OpenWRT-based management interfaces are easy to forget until they bridge into operational technology, building systems, labs, or legacy gear. The important lesson is that attackers do not have to wait for a public proof of concept if they can infer the bug from a patch.

Action:

  • Patch Lantronix EDS5000 and related exposed serial-to-IP infrastructure, especially devices still running older firmware.
  • Segment device-management paths away from user networks and the public internet.
  • Hunt for command-injection indicators, brute-force attempts, unexpected configuration changes, and new outbound traffic from device-management networks.

3. PTC Windchill and FlexPLM exploitation turns product data systems into an incident-response priority

What happened: CISA added CVE-2026-12569 in PTC Windchill and FlexPLM to the KEV catalog. NVD describes the issue as a critical RCE weakness in Windchill PDMLink and FlexPLM, and SecurityWeek reported that PTC warned of exploitation involving persistent JSP web shells.

Why it matters: PLM systems are full of design files, supplier workflows, engineering records, and partner access. For manufacturers and organizations with complex product data, a web shell on the PLM stack can become both a data-theft path and a persistence problem that survives a simple patch window.

Action:

  • Apply PTC’s fixed builds or mitigations and verify the running versions of Windchill and FlexPLM components.
  • Search for PTC-published indicators of compromise, suspicious JSP files, unexpected web roots, and abnormal child processes.
  • Rotate credentials and review partner access if exploitation or unexplained file creation is found.

4. Cisco Unified CM joins KEV after a critical SSRF flaw gets real-world urgency

What happened: CISA added CVE-2026-20230 in Cisco Unified Communications Manager to its June 25 KEV update. Cisco’s advisory describes an unauthenticated SSRF issue in Unified CM and Unified CM SME, while Horizon3.ai summarized the risk as an SSRF path that can lead to file writes and root-level compromise.

Why it matters: Voice infrastructure is often treated as business-critical but boring. That is exactly why it can be dangerous: it touches identity, call routing, contact centers, emergency communications, and internal network paths that may not get the same security review as newer cloud services.

Action:

  • Patch affected Unified CM and Unified CM SME deployments according to Cisco’s fixed-release guidance.
  • Disable or restrict WebDialer where it is not needed, and limit administrative interfaces to trusted management networks.
  • Review web logs, file-system changes, service behavior, and new accounts for signs of post-exploitation activity.

5. FortiBleed expands from leaked VPN credentials to active credential harvesting concern

What happened: The FortiBleed story widened this week as reporting from The Hacker News described a campaign targeting FortiGate firewalls with credential-harvesting pipelines that identified more than 110 million credentials. BleepingComputer also reported that CISA urged Fortinet customers to secure devices after a separate leak exposed credentials for nearly 74,000 Fortinet firewall and VPN endpoints.

Why it matters: A firewall credential is a perimeter key, not just another password in a breach list. If an organization patched Fortinet vulnerabilities but never rotated old admin, VPN, RADIUS, NTLM, Kerberos, or service credentials, it may still be reachable through valid access.

Action:

  • Rotate Fortinet administrator, VPN, RADIUS, service, and local user credentials tied to internet-facing FortiGate systems.
  • Enforce MFA and restrict management access, then verify those controls apply to the accounts attackers would actually try.
  • Review FortiGate authentication logs, configuration exports, packet-sniffer usage, and suspicious remote-access sessions.

6. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day exploitation keeps management planes in focus

What happened: Google Cloud’s Mandiant team reported zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-20245 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, where an attacker used the flaw to escalate from a compromised administrative account to root-level access. Cisco’s advisory for the affected Catalyst SD-WAN software documents the privilege-escalation issue and available fixed software in cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx.

Why it matters: SD-WAN managers sit close to routing, branch connectivity, segmentation, and policy. When attackers can reach root on the manager, defenders have to think beyond the box and validate the trust of the network configuration it controls.

Action:

  • Upgrade affected Catalyst SD-WAN Manager deployments to Cisco’s fixed software.
  • Audit administrative accounts, especially users with netadmin or write-level privileges, and rotate credentials tied to suspected compromise.
  • Review SD-WAN configuration history, file-system changes, API activity, and branch policy changes for unauthorized modifications.

7. A trusted Chrome ad blocker shows why browser extension reviews need enterprise ownership

What happened: Island researchers found that the Chrome extension Adblock for YouTube, with more than 11 million installs, had architecture that could allow remote-controlled JavaScript injection across sites, according to Island’s research. The Hacker News also covered the finding and emphasized that there was no observed malicious payload delivery, but the dormant capability and all-site browser access create real risk.

Why it matters: Browser extensions run inside the place where people access email, banking, admin consoles, SaaS apps, and internal tools. A popular extension with broad host permissions can become a client-side supply-chain problem even when it still performs the feature users installed it for.

Action:

  • Audit enterprise browser-extension inventories and remove extensions that are unnecessary, over-permissioned, abandoned, or outside policy.
  • Use allowlists for managed browsers instead of relying on install counts, store badges, or user reviews as safety signals.
  • Pay special attention to extensions with all-site access, remote configuration, ownership changes, or relationships to removed extensions.

8. A fake AI agent skill reaching 26,000 agents exposes a new supply-chain blind spot

What happened: AIR demonstrated that a fake AI agent skill could pass scanner checks by keeping the submitted package clean while relying on a mutable external link, with The Hacker News reporting that it reportedly reached roughly 26,000 agents. CSO Online summarized the same finding as a static-scanning failure where the external content could be changed after approval and after user adoption.

Why it matters: Agent skills are not just documentation. They can steer tools, read files, call APIs, and operate inside business workflows. If a scanner only checks the local package, a clean approval can turn into a bad runtime behavior once external instructions change.

Action:

  • Require central approval for third-party AI skills, plugins, and agent extensions before they can run in business environments.
  • Review external URLs, installer instructions, runtime network calls, and post-install behavior instead of trusting static package scans alone.
  • Treat AI agents as identities with least privilege, logging, revoke paths, and a clear owner for each installed capability.

9. Operation Endgame disruption is a reminder to treat infostealer exposure as credential incident response

What happened: Europol said a global cyber strike disrupted SocGholish, Amadey, and StealC malware networks, taking action against 326 servers and 142 domains. Investigators also recovered nearly 27 million stolen credentials, and Bitdefender noted the operation identified more than 41 million euros in criminal crypto assets.

Why it matters: Takedowns are useful, but they do not automatically clean up the victims. Infostealer logs can contain browser passwords, session cookies, crypto wallets, VPN credentials, SaaS tokens, and admin logins that may keep circulating after infrastructure is seized.

Action:

  • Use available notification channels, takedown intelligence, and internal telemetry to identify users and hosts tied to Amadey, StealC, or SocGholish exposure.
  • Rotate passwords and revoke sessions for affected accounts, starting with privileged, email, VPN, cloud, and finance workflows.
  • Hunt for follow-on access from initial access brokers, unusual sign-ins, OAuth abuse, mailbox rules, and endpoint persistence.

10. WhatsApp-delivered VBS files show legitimate RMM tools are still attacker favorites

What happened: Kaspersky reported an active campaign distributing malicious VBScript files through WhatsApp direct messages, with victims observed across multiple countries and the highest volume in Malaysia. The payload chain installs ManageEngine RMM Central for remote access, as detailed in Kaspersky’s Securelist writeup and summarized by The Hacker News in its coverage of the WhatsApp VBScript campaign.

Why it matters: This is the uncomfortable part of living-off-the-land abuse: the tool may be legitimate, but the install is not. Users trust files from known contacts, and defenders may trust recognized RMM names unless installation context and ownership are checked.

Action:

  • Block or alert on unauthorized RMM installations, especially ManageEngine RMM Central or Endpoint Central appearing outside approved deployment paths.
  • Train users that unexpected business documents over WhatsApp, even from known contacts, need verification before opening on desktop systems.
  • Review UAC tampering, script execution, new services, and outbound connections tied to suspicious WhatsApp-delivered attachments.

Closing Notes

The priority stack this week is clear: internet-facing management systems first, then credential exposure, then the trusted tools people install because they make work easier. Patch quickly, but do not let patching become the finish line. Verify the asset, rotate the credential, check for persistence, and tighten the policy that allowed the exposure to matter in the first place.

item.title: AI Made the Call, but Your Company Still Owns the Failure
item.xhtml:a: AI Made the Call, but Your Company Still Owns the Failure

xhtml:img.alt: A security operations center with an AI system making decisions while several human and corporate figures are connected by lines representing shared responsibility.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: When an AI security tool misses an intrusion, blocks production, leaks sensitive data, or runs the wrong remediation, liability does not disappear into the algorithm. It follows the people and companies that built, sold, configured, approved, and relied on it.
item.content:encoded:
AI can make the recommendation, but it cannot sign the contract, accept the risk, or explain the failure to a regulator.

Imagine an AI-powered security platform receives an alert about unusual administrative activity.

The system analyzes the event, compares it against previous behavior, and decides it is probably a false positive. It automatically lowers the severity, suppresses similar alerts, and closes the case without sending it to a human analyst.

Two days later, the company discovers that the activity was part of a ransomware intrusion.

Who is responsible?

Is it the company that built the AI model? The security vendor that included it in its platform? The MSP that configured the system? The analyst who trusted the recommendation? Or the customer that approved automated alert closure in the first place?

The honest answer is that liability could reach several of them.

AI is moving beyond summarizing alerts and generating queries. I have written before about where AI can fit into SOC workflows, but the risk changes once security products use it to prioritize incidents, recommend containment, identify malicious behavior, write remediation scripts, disable accounts, quarantine devices, and make other decisions that can materially affect an organization.

That creates an uncomfortable question the cybersecurity industry has not fully answered:

When an AI system makes the wrong security decision, who owns the failure?

This article discusses general cybersecurity, governance, and liability considerations. It is not legal advice.

The AI is not going to be the defendant

The first thing to understand is that the AI itself is not likely to be the party held responsible.

It does not sign contracts. It does not purchase insurance. It does not approve risk. It does not have professional obligations to a client. It also cannot sit across from an executive team, regulator, insurer, or angry customer and explain why it missed an intrusion.

The responsibility remains with the people and organizations surrounding the technology.

That may include:

  • The AI or security product vendor
  • A foundation-model or threat-intelligence provider
  • The MSP, MSSP, consultant, or systems integrator
  • The organization deploying the system
  • The employees approving or acting on its output
  • Executives responsible for cybersecurity governance
  • Other third parties involved in the service chain

The difficult part will be determining how responsibility should be divided.

Shared responsibility does not mean equal responsibility.

There is no AI exemption from existing law

The lack of one comprehensive federal AI liability law does not mean organizations can deploy AI without consequences.

The Federal Trade Commission has stated that there is no AI exemption from existing laws. Existing rules involving unfair or deceptive practices, privacy, data security, discrimination, contractual obligations, and professional negligence can still apply when AI is involved.

The FTC has already taken action against companies accused of overstating the effectiveness of AI products. Its case involving Evolv Technologies focused on allegedly misleading claims about an AI-powered security screening system. In another case, the agency challenged unsupported accuracy claims made by an AI detection company.

Those cases were not about an AI SOC platform missing ransomware, but the lesson transfers directly to cybersecurity vendors.

If a vendor claims its AI can autonomously detect threats, eliminate false positives, replace analyst review, or stop attacks before damage occurs, it needs evidence supporting those claims.

Calling something “AI-powered” does not lower the standard. In some cases, it may increase the expectations placed on the company selling it.

Europe is beginning to define the responsibility chain

The European Union is taking a more explicit approach.

Where an AI system falls within the high-risk classifications of the EU AI Act, the law establishes responsibilities for both providers and deployers.

Providers may be responsible for areas such as risk management, technical documentation, logging, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, and designing systems so they can be effectively overseen by humans.

Deployers also have responsibilities. They must use covered systems according to their instructions, assign oversight to people with appropriate competence and authority, monitor operation, and respond when risks or unexpected behavior appear.

This distinction matters because the company using an AI system cannot simply blame the vendor if it ignored documented limitations, removed safeguards, provided poor-quality input, or deployed the tool outside its intended purpose.

The EU’s updated Product Liability Directive also treats commercial software, including AI systems, as products for product-liability purposes. It recognizes that software updates, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, connected services, and a system’s ability to continue learning may affect whether a product is considered defective.

However, it is not a blanket compensation mechanism for every cybersecurity incident. Its covered damages focus primarily on harm to natural persons, certain property damage, and destruction or corruption of data not used for professional purposes. Pure economic losses and business data may still need to be addressed through contracts, negligence claims, privacy law, or other national liability regimes.

The larger direction is still clear: AI is not being treated as an accountability escape hatch.

Liability will follow control, knowledge, promises, and cause

After an AI-related cybersecurity failure, four questions will likely shape the investigation.

QuestionWhat it reveals
Who controlled the decision?Which party configured the system, granted permissions, selected the automation level, or approved the action
Who knew about the limitation?Whether known false-negative rates, unsupported environments, model weaknesses, or prior failures were disclosed or ignored
What was promised?Whether marketing, contracts, SLAs, documentation, or sales statements overstated what the system could do
What actually caused the damage?Whether the harm resulted from a defective product, poor implementation, bad data, misuse, lack of oversight, or several failures together

That is why the answer will rarely be as simple as “the vendor is liable” or “the customer accepted the risk.”

Cybersecurity services are already built on shared responsibility. AI makes that relationship harder because one party may build the model, another may integrate it, an MSP may configure it, and the customer may decide how much authority it receives.

When the vendor may be responsible

The AI or security vendor could face exposure when the failure comes from the design or operation of the product itself.

That could include:

  • Materially misleading accuracy or performance claims
  • Failure to disclose known limitations
  • Insecure model interfaces or integrations
  • A lack of reasonable logging or auditability
  • Failure to address known vulnerabilities
  • Unsafe default settings
  • An AI system operating outside documented restrictions
  • Updates that materially change behavior without adequate notice
  • A system marketed for autonomous response that cannot safely perform that function

A vendor should not be able to advertise a platform as autonomous, intelligent, and capable of replacing human work, then retreat to “AI can make mistakes” after an incident.

Warnings and disclaimers matter, but they should not erase the core promises used to sell the product.

When the MSP, MSSP, or integrator may be responsible

This is where the issue becomes especially important for managed service providers.

An MSP may not have created the model, but it may have selected the product, configured the integrations, written the response playbooks, set the thresholds, granted permissions, and sold the resulting service to the customer.

That is part of why AI exposes operational debt inside MSP security stacks. Weak ownership, unclear escalation paths, and untested response workflows become much harder to defend once an AI system is making or accelerating decisions.

If the MSP markets the service as 24/7 AI-powered detection and response, the customer is not going to begin its complaint with the model developer. The customer is going to contact the MSP.

Exposure could increase when the provider:

  • Enables automated containment without adequate testing
  • Fails to follow the vendor’s deployment guidance
  • Does not validate the system against the customer’s environment
  • Removes human review to reduce staffing costs
  • Ignores recurring false positives or false negatives
  • Gives the tool unnecessary administrative privileges
  • Fails to notify the customer about known limitations
  • Does not preserve the logs needed to investigate a failure
  • Promises an outcome that is not supported by the underlying service

The service agreement will matter, but so will the MSP’s actual conduct.

A limitation-of-liability clause will not make poor implementation disappear. It may limit damages, depending on the contract and applicable law, but it does not change what happened.

When the customer may be responsible

The organization deploying the system also owns part of the risk.

A customer may increase its exposure if it disables recommended telemetry, refuses required security controls, ignores warnings, uses the system outside its intended purpose, or grants autonomous authority without appropriate review.

The organization also decides whether the AI is advisory or operational.

There is a major difference between asking an AI system to summarize an alert and allowing it to:

  • Disable a user account
  • Revoke sessions
  • Isolate an endpoint
  • Block network traffic
  • Delete a file
  • Modify firewall rules
  • Rotate credentials
  • Execute a generated script

Once an organization gives the system authority to change the environment, the organization has made a governance decision, not merely a technology purchase.

That decision should be documented, tested, approved, and reviewed like any other material security control.

“Human in the loop” is not automatically a defense

Many vendors and organizations point to human oversight as the answer.

That is important, but the phrase is becoming almost meaningless.

A human is not providing meaningful oversight when they receive hundreds of AI-generated recommendations and are expected to approve each one within seconds. That is not review. It is a rubber stamp with a username attached to it.

Meaningful oversight requires the person to have:

  • Enough information to understand the recommendation
  • Access to the supporting evidence
  • Time to challenge the conclusion
  • Training on the system’s limitations
  • Authority to reject or reverse the action
  • A reliable way to stop the system
  • Protection from being punished for slowing down automation when something looks wrong

Human oversight is not a control when the human cannot realistically investigate the decision.

Organizations should also watch for automation bias. Once a tool develops a reputation for being correct, analysts may stop independently evaluating its conclusions.

That creates a dangerous feedback loop. The AI becomes trusted because people rarely challenge it, and people rarely challenge it because it is considered trusted.

How different failures could distribute responsibility

The exact answer will depend on the facts, contracts, jurisdiction, and damage involved. Still, several common scenarios show how responsibility could be divided.

The AI misses an intrusion

The vendor may face questions if it made unsupported detection claims or concealed known limitations.

The MSP or MSSP may face questions if it promised continuous monitoring but allowed the AI to close alerts without meaningful analyst review.

The customer may share responsibility if it disabled telemetry, rejected recommended services, or ignored repeated warnings.

The AI causes an outage during containment

The integrator or deploying organization may be responsible if it granted excessive permissions, skipped testing, or failed to create rollback procedures.

The vendor may carry more responsibility if the product ignored configured restrictions or performed an action outside its documented behavior.

An AI-generated remediation script deletes data

The organization executing an untested script may own much of the immediate failure, especially if there was no backup or change-control process.

The vendor’s responsibility may increase if the system was specifically marketed as safe for autonomous code execution and the failure resulted from a product defect rather than an unpredictable output that required review.

Sensitive security data is exposed to an external model

The customer, MSP, or employee may be responsible for sending confidential logs, credentials, client information, or incident data to an unapproved service.

That is the same visibility problem behind shadow AI becoming the new shadow IT: useful tools appear faster than the organization’s review, data, identity, and logging controls.

The model provider may face responsibility if it violated its stated retention, confidentiality, security, or training commitments.

In each situation, several failures can exist at the same time.

The contract will decide the first fight

Before anyone reaches a courtroom, the parties will probably reach for their contracts.

Organizations purchasing or reselling AI-powered security products should review more than price, uptime, and license counts.

The agreement should clearly address:

  • Which functions use AI
  • Whether AI decisions are advisory or autonomous
  • The documented performance limitations
  • Required human-review points
  • Data retention and model-training practices
  • Ownership of prompts, outputs, logs, and incident data
  • Notification requirements after security or model failures
  • Access to evidence needed for an investigation
  • Changes to the underlying model or service
  • Responsibility for third-party models and data sources
  • Indemnification and liability limitations
  • Cyber, technology errors and omissions, and professional-liability coverage

A traditional uptime SLA may be nearly useless in this situation.

The platform may have been available 99.99 percent of the time while making the wrong decision during every minute that mattered.

Decision quality, logging, response time, escalation, false negatives, and the ability to recover from automated actions may be more important than basic availability.

A defensible AI security program needs evidence

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary, but it provides a useful structure for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks. NIST is also developing a Cyber AI Profile focused on securing AI systems, using AI for cyber defense, and defending against AI-enabled attacks.

This is also where the broader GRC muscle matters. If you already have one risk-based governance program that maps controls to multiple frameworks, AI accountability becomes another risk scenario to govern instead of a completely separate paperwork universe.

Following a framework does not guarantee immunity from liability.

It does, however, help an organization demonstrate that it identified risks, assigned ownership, evaluated the system, and implemented controls instead of blindly deploying whatever the vendor labeled as intelligent.

Organizations using AI in security operations should be able to produce evidence showing:

  1. What the system was allowed to do. Maintain an inventory of AI capabilities, integrations, privileges, and autonomous actions.

  2. Who approved the authority. Document who accepted the risk and why the selected automation level was appropriate.

  3. How it was tested. Validate the system against the organization’s actual environment, not only the vendor’s demonstration data.

  4. What information informed each decision. Preserve relevant prompts, model versions, telemetry, recommendations, tool actions, approvals, and overrides.

  5. How humans can intervene. Define clear escalation paths, approval thresholds, stop mechanisms, and emergency shutdown procedures.

  6. How actions can be reversed. Maintain backups, rollback processes, manual alternatives, and tested recovery procedures.

  7. How performance is monitored. Track false positives, false negatives, drift, unexplained decisions, failed actions, and analyst overrides.

  8. How incidents involving AI will be handled. Update incident-response plans so the organization knows how to preserve evidence, disable automation, notify affected parties, and investigate the model’s role.

For MSPs, documentation should also show which controls the client accepted, declined, or changed.

That documentation should not be treated as a way to blame the customer. It is a way to make the responsibility boundary clear before an incident forces everyone to argue about it.

Do not outsource accountability with the workload

AI can help overwhelmed security teams process more data, investigate incidents faster, and respond at a scale humans cannot manage alone.

That does not mean it should operate without boundaries.

The more authority an organization delegates to an AI system, the more attention it must give to testing, logging, oversight, contracts, recovery, and accountability.

That is especially true for agentic systems. Once AI can use tools, call APIs, and take action across business workflows, it becomes an identity, access, and accountability problem, not just another chatbot risk.

The companies that run into the most trouble will probably not be the ones that used AI.

They will be the ones that could not explain:

  • Why they trusted it
  • What it was allowed to do
  • Who approved it
  • Whether anyone monitored it
  • How they tested it
  • What happened when it failed

AI can automate a security decision. It cannot own the consequences.

Do not give an AI system more authority than your organization can audit, explain, and reverse.

item.title: CybersecKyle Security How-To Series: Home Network and Devices, Part 4 - IoT Quarantine and DNS Choices
item.xhtml:a: CybersecKyle Security How-To Series: Home Network and Devices, Part 4 - IoT Quarantine and DNS Choices

xhtml:img.alt: Network security themed image representing protected devices and safer home network decisions.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: A practical home network guide for keeping smart devices in their own lane, choosing a safer DNS setup, filtering obvious junk, and validating that IoT gear cannot wander into private devices.
item.content:encoded:
I am back with Season 2, Part 4 of the Home Network and Devices track in my CybersecKyle Security How-To Series. This time we are putting smart devices in their own lane and making a sane DNS choice without turning the house into a troubleshooting hobby.

Smart devices are convenient little chaos machines.

I am not anti-smart-home. I like convenience. I like automation. I like not getting up to turn off a lamp when I am already comfortable. But I also do not want a bargain-bin camera, old TV, or mystery plug sitting beside my work laptop like they have earned the same level of trust.

They have not.

The point of IoT quarantine is not paranoia. It is basic network manners. Devices should get the access they need and not much more.

DNS is similar. A good DNS setup can block obvious junk, reduce tracking, and make the network calmer. A bad DNS setup can break apps, hide the real problem, and make everyone blame “the internet” when the filter is actually the issue.

So we are going to keep this practical.

What you are building

By the end of this guide, you should have:

  • A list of smart devices in your home
  • A separate IoT or guest network where practical
  • Risky devices moved off the trusted main network
  • A DNS provider chosen on purpose
  • Basic filtering enabled if it fits your household
  • A validation test that proves private devices are not reachable from the IoT lane

This is the next step after router sanity and guest Wi-Fi. If you have not done that yet, start there.

What belongs in the IoT lane

I put these devices on an IoT or guest network whenever it is practical:

  • Smart TVs
  • Streaming sticks
  • Smart speakers
  • Cameras and doorbells
  • Smart plugs and bulbs
  • Thermostats
  • Appliances
  • Game consoles if they do not need trusted local access
  • Guest devices you do not manage

I usually keep these on the trusted network:

  • Your primary laptop
  • Your phone
  • Work devices
  • NAS or file server
  • Printer if trusted devices need local printing
  • Home server dashboards
  • Admin devices used to manage the router

There will be exceptions. HomeKit, Chromecast, AirPlay, Sonos, printers, and some hubs may need local discovery. Exceptions are fine. Accidental flat networks are not.

Step 1: Inventory the weird stuff

Open your router app and make a quick list.

Device:
Type:
Owner:
Current network:
Needs local access to:
Cloud account used:
Last firmware update checked:
Can move to IoT/guest network:

Do not try to solve everything while inventorying. Just map what exists.

If you see unknown devices, investigate before blocking wildly. Randomized MAC addresses and terrible device names can make normal devices look suspicious.

Unknown does not always mean hostile. It does mean worth checking.

Step 2: Pick the quarantine lane your router supports

Use the best option your gear gives you.

OptionGood forWatch out for
Dedicated IoT networkRouters and mesh systems that support a specific smart-device SSIDLocal discovery rules may be limited or unclear
Guest networkMost home routersMake sure local network access is disabled
VLANsPower users with prosumer or business gearEasy to overbuild and hard to troubleshoot if rushed

If your router only supports one guest network, use that. If it supports IoT mode, try that. If you have VLAN-capable gear and understand firewall rules, great. Keep notes.

The goal is not to win a network design contest. The goal is to stop low-trust devices from having free access to high-trust devices.

Step 3: Move devices in small batches

Do not move everything at once.

Start with the easy wins:

  • Smart TV
  • Streaming stick
  • Smart plugs
  • Smart bulbs
  • Old tablet used as a controller
  • Guest devices

Then test normal use.

If a device breaks, write down what broke. Did the mobile app stop seeing it? Did casting fail? Did printing fail? Did a hub lose control of a device?

This is where people get frustrated and undo the whole project. Do not undo the whole project. Decide whether that one device needs an exception.

Good exceptions are narrow:

  • A specific controller can reach a specific printer
  • A phone can discover a specific speaker
  • A hub can talk to its devices

Bad exceptions are broad:

  • Guest network can access the whole LAN
  • Every IoT device can see every private device
  • Router admin is reachable from every network

Step 4: Choose DNS on purpose

DNS turns names into addresses. Your devices ask DNS where example.com lives, and DNS answers.

Changing DNS can improve privacy, block known malicious domains, or filter adult content. It can also break things if you choose a provider that is too aggressive or configure it inconsistently.

Common options:

  • ISP DNS: usually works, but may be less privacy-friendly or less filtered
  • Cloudflare: fast, simple public DNS options
  • Quad9: security-focused blocking of known malicious domains
  • NextDNS or Control D: customizable filtering with dashboards
  • Pi-hole or AdGuard Home: local filtering you manage yourself

For most people, I would pick one of two paths:

  1. Use a reputable public DNS provider at the router and keep it simple.
  2. Use a customizable DNS provider if you actually want to manage allow/block lists.

Do not deploy a local filtering box if you do not want to maintain it. A broken Pi-hole becomes “the internet is down” very quickly.

Step 5: Filter gently first

Start with security filtering, not maximum blocking.

Block:

  • Known malware domains
  • Known phishing domains
  • Newly suspicious domains if your provider supports it and false positives are tolerable
  • Adult content only if that is a household requirement

Be careful with:

  • Aggressive ad blocking at the network layer
  • Social media blocking
  • Tracking protection that breaks login flows
  • Blocking entire countries or TLDs without a reason

Filtering should reduce noise, not become a second job.

When something breaks, do not immediately disable the whole setup. Check the logs if available. Add a narrow allow rule if the domain is legitimate. Document why you allowed it.

Step 6: Protect router and DNS admin access

If DNS filtering has a dashboard, protect that account.

Use:

  • Unique password
  • MFA or passkey where available
  • Recovery email you control
  • Limited admin sharing

If someone can change your DNS filtering, they can weaken it, spy through logs, or make the network miserable.

Treat the DNS dashboard like security infrastructure because it is.

Validation drills: prove the quarantine works

Drill 1: IoT internet test

Connect a smart device to the IoT or guest network and confirm it still reaches the internet.

Expected result:

The device works for normal internet-connected features.

Drill 2: Private device access test

From an IoT or guest device, try to reach:

  • Router admin page
  • Printer web page
  • NAS
  • Home server dashboard
  • Another laptop

Expected result:

The IoT or guest device cannot reach private network resources.

Drill 3: DNS leak sanity check

From a trusted device, use your DNS provider’s test page or a DNS leak test to confirm queries are using the provider you configured.

Expected result:

DNS queries use the intended provider.

Drill 4: Blocking test

Use your DNS provider’s safe test domain if it offers one.

Expected result:

The provider blocks its known test domain and normal sites still load.

Drill 5: Exception review

List every exception you made.

Expected result:

Every exception has a device, reason, and owner.

IoT quarantine and DNS checklist

IoT and DNS Checklist

Inventory
[ ] Router device list reviewed
[ ] Smart devices identified
[ ] Unknown devices investigated
[ ] Device names cleaned up where possible

Segmentation
[ ] IoT or guest network selected
[ ] Local network access disabled for guests where possible
[ ] Smart TVs moved off main network
[ ] Cameras moved off main network where practical
[ ] Smart plugs, bulbs, and speakers moved where practical
[ ] Exceptions documented

DNS
[ ] DNS provider chosen on purpose
[ ] Router DNS configured if appropriate
[ ] Filtering level selected
[ ] Admin account protected
[ ] Allow/block changes documented

Validation
[ ] IoT devices still reach internet
[ ] IoT devices cannot reach router admin
[ ] IoT devices cannot reach private devices
[ ] DNS provider test passes
[ ] Normal household apps still work

Final thought

Smart devices do not need to be treated like villains. They just do not need the keys to the whole house.

Give them internet. Give them the local access they truly need. Keep them away from the devices and files that matter more.

Then make DNS boring and intentional.

The best version of this setup is not flashy. It is a home network where the cheap camera can do camera things, the TV can stream, the laptop can work, and none of them get more trust than they earned.

item.title: The Gatekeeping Problem in IT and Cybersecurity Hiring
item.xhtml:a: The Gatekeeping Problem in IT and Cybersecurity Hiring

xhtml:img.alt: The Gatekeeping Problem in IT and Cybersecurity Hiring

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: IT and cybersecurity hiring often says it wants people who can learn, then filters candidates by exact tools, certs, and prior job titles. That mismatch hurts job seekers and employers.
item.content:encoded:
IT and cybersecurity hiring has a gatekeeping problem.

I do not mean that every requirement is unfair. Some jobs really do need someone who has touched the system before. If a company needs a senior identity engineer, a cloud security architect, or someone who can lead incident response during a live breach, it is reasonable to ask for specific experience. Nobody wants a person learning the basics of firewall policy, privilege escalation, or endpoint containment for the first time while production is actively on fire.

That is not the part that bothers me.

The part that bothers me is how often the industry talks about needing more people, then builds hiring filters that only reward people who already had access to the exact tools, titles, and environments the job is supposed to train them into.

That is where the gatekeeping starts.

A degree in IT, cybersecurity, computer science, information systems, or a related field should mean something. It does not mean the person is automatically ready for every technical job. It does not replace hands-on experience. It does not prove judgment under pressure. But it does show that the person can stick with a structured learning path, absorb unfamiliar concepts, write, troubleshoot, research, meet deadlines, and build enough foundation to keep learning.

That should matter in a field where the work changes constantly.

Instead, a lot of candidates find out that the degree is treated like a checkbox at best. Employers may say they want problem solvers, learners, and people with potential, but the actual posting asks for a very specific stack: three years of Azure, two years of Sentinel, CrowdStrike experience, Okta, Palo Alto, Python, PowerShell, vulnerability management, incident response, compliance, networking, Linux, Windows Server, and a certification or two. Then the job is labeled entry-level or junior because the salary band says it is.

That mismatch is brutal.

The degree is not worthless, but it is not enough by itself

This is the part that needs some honesty on both sides.

Job seekers are not wrong to feel frustrated when they spent years earning a degree and still get screened out for not having one narrow tool on their resume. That degree likely required networking, operating systems, databases, programming, security fundamentals, project work, writing, and plenty of learning under pressure. Those are real signals.

But employers are also not completely wrong to want evidence that someone can do the job in the environment they actually run.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes information security analysts as typically needing a bachelor’s degree in a computer science field, related work experience, and sometimes professional certification. BLS also projects 29% growth for information security analyst roles from 2024 to 2034, which is much faster than the average occupation. So the demand story is real.

The problem is that “demand” does not automatically create clean on-ramps.

Cybersecurity is especially awkward because many security jobs are not truly entry-level. A SOC analyst needs enough networking knowledge to know what looks weird. A vulnerability analyst needs enough systems context to understand why a patch is risky or urgent. A GRC analyst needs enough business and technical awareness to know whether a control is meaningful or theater. Even junior security work benefits from previous IT exposure.

That reality should shape training paths, internships, apprenticeships, and job design.

It should not become an excuse to call a job “entry-level” while asking for someone who already sounds mid-career.

Skills-based hiring sounds good until it becomes keyword-based hiring

There is a difference between skills-based hiring and keyword-based hiring.

Skills-based hiring asks, “Can this person do the work, learn the missing pieces, and grow into the role?”

Keyword-based hiring asks, “Did this person use the exact nouns in our job description?”

Those are not the same thing.

The Burning Glass Institute and Harvard Business School have pointed out that a lot of employers announced a move away from degree requirements, but the actual hiring change has been slower and less consistent than the headlines made it sound. That tracks with what many job seekers feel. The paper ceiling may move in one place while another wall gets built out of tools, certifications, years of experience, and applicant tracking filters.

In cybersecurity, that can get weird fast.

A candidate might understand SIEM concepts, log sources, alert triage, basic detection logic, and incident documentation, but get passed over because they used Splunk in a lab and the job wants Microsoft Sentinel in production. Another candidate might understand identity fundamentals, MFA, conditional access concepts, least privilege, and account recovery risk, but get filtered out because they have not administered Okta specifically. Someone else might have years of help desk, endpoint, and scripting experience, but lose to a resume parser because their title was not “security analyst.”

That is not skills-based hiring.

That is tool-name matching.

Tools matter. Production experience matters. But if the hiring process cannot tell the difference between a missing tool name and a missing skill, it is going to reject people who could have become strong employees with a reasonable ramp.

Entry-level should not mean “already validated by someone else”

The entry-level cyber problem is often an ownership problem.

Everyone wants entry-level talent that someone else already trained.

Colleges are expected to produce job-ready graduates. Bootcamps are expected to compress years of experience into months. Certification vendors are expected to prove competence with exams. Home labs are expected to stand in for production exposure. And when all of that still does not feel like enough, employers ask for prior experience anyway.

That creates a ridiculous loop:

  1. You need experience to get the job.
  2. You need the job to get experience.
  3. You try to build proof outside the job.
  4. Employers say the proof is not the same as real experience.
  5. You are back at step one.

This is where the frustration turns into something unhealthy.

The ISC2 2025 Cybersecurity Hiring Trends Report is useful because it says the quiet part out loud. ISC2 noted that more than a third of hiring managers wanted advanced certifications or unrealistic skills for entry and junior-level candidates. The same report also points to internships and apprenticeships as important sources for early-career talent, and says some hiring managers are looking beyond traditional cybersecurity and computer science backgrounds.

That is the direction we need more of.

If an organization wants junior people, it has to build junior roles. That means tighter scope, clearer expectations, better mentorship, documented workflows, and a realistic training period. It means being honest about what must be known on day one and what can be learned in the first 30, 60, or 90 days.

If the team cannot support that, then it should stop calling the role entry-level.

The resume pressure is a symptom, not just a character flaw

I am not going to tell people to lie on resumes.

Do not do that.

It can burn your reputation, fail a background check, put you into a job you cannot actually perform, and make every future interview harder. In cybersecurity especially, trust matters. If the first signal you send is that you are willing to misrepresent access, experience, or credentials, that is a bad foundation.

But I also think it is too easy to moralize about resume dishonesty without looking at the system that creates the pressure.

Monster’s 2026 Credibility Gap Report found that 13% of U.S. job seekers admitted to recently lying or including misleading information on a resume. Among those who misrepresented something, the most common areas included employment dates, responsibilities, skills or tool proficiency, job titles, results, education credentials, and certifications.

That does not make lying acceptable.

It does show what people feel pressured to stretch.

If every posting demands exact experience, candidates start translating their background into the language the system rewards. Some do that ethically by reframing transferable skills. Some cross the line. The more rigid and unrealistic the filter becomes, the more tempting it is for a desperate person to write the resume the system seems to want instead of the resume that honestly describes what they have done.

Again, that is not a defense of lying.

It is a warning sign.

Hiring systems teach candidates what they believe matters. If the lesson is “only exact keywords survive,” candidates will optimize for exact keywords. If the lesson is “we value demonstrated learning, adjacent experience, labs, writing, troubleshooting, and honest growth,” candidates have a better path to show what they can actually do.

Gatekeeping hides behind risk

Some gatekeeping is obvious.

“You need a degree from this kind of school.”

“You need five years of experience for a junior role.”

“You need a CISSP before you have even had enough professional experience to hold the certification cleanly.”

That stuff is easy to criticize.

The harder version hides behind risk.

Hiring managers are scared of making a bad hire. Security teams are already overloaded. Nobody wants to spend months training someone who leaves. Nobody wants to hire a person who cannot handle the work. Nobody wants to explain to leadership why the new analyst missed something important.

Those concerns are real.

But risk cuts both ways.

There is risk in hiring someone inexperienced and unsupported. There is also risk in never building a pipeline. There is risk in filtering for the same narrow profile over and over. There is risk in understaffing teams because nobody matches the fantasy posting. There is risk in burning out the few people who do meet the bar because the organization never figured out how to grow the next layer.

The CyberSeek heat map continues to show hundreds of thousands of cybersecurity-related job postings in the United States, while also tracking supply and demand across roles, regions, certifications, and the NICE Framework categories. That data is a reminder that the problem is not only whether people are interested in cybersecurity. The problem is matching real people to real work in a way that does not collapse into wish lists.

Gatekeeping feels safe because it narrows the funnel.

Sometimes it just narrows the imagination.

Better job descriptions would separate foundations from preferences

One practical fix is simple, but not easy: write job descriptions like someone actually understands the job.

Separate requirements into three groups:

  • What the person must know on day one
  • What they can learn with support
  • What would be nice but should not decide the whole search

For example, a junior SOC role might require basic networking, Windows and Linux familiarity, security fundamentals, documentation discipline, and the ability to explain an alert investigation clearly. Experience with a specific SIEM can be a preference. Experience with the exact EDR can be trainable. Prior production incident response can be a bonus instead of a hard gate.

That is not lowering the bar.

That is naming the bar correctly.

NIST’s NICE Framework exists for exactly this kind of clarity. It gives employers, educators, and workers a common language for cybersecurity work, knowledge, skills, job descriptions, and candidate assessment. That kind of framework is useful because it pushes the conversation away from vague titles and toward actual tasks.

If a posting says “security analyst,” that can mean almost anything.

If it says the person will triage phishing reports, review endpoint detections, escalate suspicious identity events, document timelines, update tickets, and follow playbooks, then candidates and hiring teams both get a clearer picture.

Clarity is more humane.

It is also better security.

Job seekers need a better way to show transferable skill

This is not only on employers.

Job seekers also need to learn how to translate their experience without inflating it.

If your degree gave you networking, Linux, scripting, risk, policy, or database experience, do not just list the degree and hope someone infers the rest. Pull the useful parts forward. If you built a lab, write down what you built, what broke, what you learned, and how you validated it. If you worked help desk, connect that to identity, endpoint troubleshooting, ticket discipline, user communication, escalation, and root-cause thinking.

Do not say you managed a SIEM if you watched a few videos.

Do say you built a home lab that ingested Windows event logs, wrote basic detection queries, investigated failed login patterns, and documented findings.

Do not say you administered enterprise Azure if you only used a student tenant.

Do say you configured a test tenant, created users and groups, tested MFA policies, reviewed sign-in logs, and learned how conditional access decisions are evaluated.

That distinction matters.

The goal is not to make your experience sound bigger than it was. The goal is to make the learning visible enough that a reasonable employer can see the bridge between where you are and where the role needs you to go.

Employers should hire for learning velocity, not only inventory

The uncomfortable truth is that nobody in IT or cybersecurity is fully current forever.

Tools change. Licensing changes. Threats change. Cloud platforms change. Attackers change. Business priorities change. Compliance expectations change. Even the same tool can behave differently depending on how the environment is designed.

So yes, hire for skills.

But do not confuse a static inventory of tools with long-term ability.

A good candidate can learn, communicate, troubleshoot, document, ask useful questions, admit uncertainty, and keep going when the answer is not obvious. A good candidate can connect a technical problem to operational impact. A good candidate knows when to escalate, when to research, and when to stop guessing.

Those traits are harder to measure than “two years of CrowdStrike.”

They are also the traits that decide whether someone keeps growing after the hire.

Degrees, certifications, labs, previous jobs, portfolios, and interviews are all just signals. None of them are perfect. The hiring process should be trying to combine those signals into a picture of capability and growth, not using each one as a separate gate to slam shut.

The industry cannot complain about the pipeline while blocking the doors

Cybersecurity keeps saying it needs people.

IT keeps saying it needs people.

Businesses keep saying technology risk is growing.

Then too many postings ask for the already-formed version of the employee they never invested in creating.

That is the contradiction.

If we want better hiring, we need to stop pretending the only safe candidate is the one who already did the job somewhere else. We need more honest job descriptions, better apprenticeships and internships, stronger mentorship, clearer junior roles, and interviews that test reasoning instead of memorized tool trivia. We need to respect degrees as one signal of learning without pretending they replace practical work. We need to respect practical experience without turning every tool name into a wall.

Most of all, we need to stop treating potential like a liability.

Potential is not enough by itself. It needs structure, support, and accountability.

But without it, the field just keeps recycling the same experienced people until they burn out, leave, or become the next impossible requirement on a job posting.

That is not a talent strategy.

That is gatekeeping with a staffing problem attached.
